claims.evidence: This claim is based on computational modeling results presented in the study.

claims.claim: Hallucinations and delusions are burdensome symptoms that typically manifest together as the psychotic syndrome of schizophrenia.
claims.source: Hallucinations and delusions are burdensome symptoms that typically manifest together as the psychotic syndrome of schizophrenia.
claims.evidence: This is a statement based on established clinical knowledge about schizophrenia.

claims.claim: Perceptual-inference models of psychosis suggest that hallucinations and delusions result from alterations in the updating of internal models of the environment used to make inferences about external sensory events and their causes.
claims.source: Perceptual-inference models of psychosis suggest that these symptoms result from alterations in the updating of internal models of the environment that are used to make inferences about external sensory events and their causes (Adams et al., 2013; Horga and Abi-Dargham, 2019; Sterzer et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior theoretical work.

claims.claim: Perceptual-inference models of psychosis are receiving increasing empirical support.
claims.source: These models are receiving increasing empirical support (Adams et al., 2018; Baker et al., 2019; Cassidy et al., 2018; Davies et al., 2018; Powers et al., 2017; Teufel et al., 2015)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to empirical studies.

claims.claim: Current theories do not provide a satisfactory explanation for how hallucinations and delusions tend to co-occur but sometimes manifest in isolation.
claims.source: yet current theories do not provide a satisfactory explanation for how hallucinations and delusions tend to co-occur but sometimes manifest in isolation.
claims.evidence: This is an assessment of the current state of theoretical models based on inference from the literature.

claims.claim: Hallucinations and delusions may share a common neurobiological mechanism while simultaneously depending on symptom-specific pathways.
claims.source: This suggests that these psychotic symptoms may share a common neurobiological mechanism while simultaneously depending on symptom-specific pathways.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that symptoms co-occur but can also manifest in isolation.

claims.claim: Alterations at higher levels of the perceptual-inference hierarchy may drive delusions.
claims.source: One possibility is that alterations at higher levels—supporting inferences on abstract hidden states like someone's intentions—may drive delusions
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis based on hierarchical perceptual-inference models, supported by citations.

claims.claim: Alterations at lower levels of the perceptual-inference hierarchy may drive hallucinations.
claims.source: and alterations at lower levels—supporting inferences about lower level features of stimuli such as stimulus presence or absence—may drive hallucinations (Baker et al., 2019; Davies et al., 2018; Horga and Abi-Dargham, 2019; Powers et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis based on hierarchical perceptual-inference models, supported by citations.

claims.claim: Alterations at any level of the perceptual-inference hierarchy may naturally propagate throughout the interdependent levels of the hierarchy.
claims.source: In addition to these symptom-specific pathways, alterations at any level may naturally propagate throughout the interdependent levels of the hierarchy (Chaudhuri et al., 2015), potentially explaining symptom co-occurrence.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a computational modeling study.

claims.claim: Neural systems supporting inference feature a hierarchical architecture of timescales that mirrors the hierarchical temporal dynamics of natural environments.
claims.source: Importantly, neural systems supporting inference are thought to feature a hierarchical architecture of timescales that mirrors the hierarchical temporal dynamics of natural environments, where rapidly changing events are typically nested within slower changing contexts (Kiebel et al., 2008; Kiebel, 2009).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to theoretical work on hierarchical temporal dynamics.

claims.claim: Higher level inferences pertaining to slower changing contexts require neural systems with the ability to integrate information over longer periods.
claims.source: Thus, higher level inferences pertaining to slower changing contexts require neural systems with the ability to integrate information over longer periods, an ability consistent with the persistent neuronal activity that characterizes higher level regions (Major and Tank, 2004; Mazurek et al., 2003).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to empirical studies on neural integration.

claims.claim: A hierarchy of neural timescales is observed in single-neuron recordings in non-human primates.
claims.source: A hierarchy of neural timescales is observed in both single-neuron recordings in non-human primates (Murray et al., 2014)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to an empirical study.

claims.claim: A hierarchy of neural timescales is observed in functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) recordings in humans.
claims.source: and functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) recordings in humans (Hasson et al., 2015; Hasson et al., 2008; Honey et al., 2012; Lerner et al., 2011; Stephens et al., 2013)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to empirical fMRI studies.

claims.claim: A hierarchy of neural timescales is recapitulated by a large-scale biophysical model.
claims.source: and is recapitulated by a large-scale biophysical model (Chaudhuri et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a computational modeling study.

claims.claim: A newly developed method based on resting-state fMRI was validated against electroencephalography (EEG) and captures a hierarchy of intrinsic neural timescales (INT).
claims.source: Furthermore, a newly developed method based on resting-state fMRI that was validated against electroencephalography (EEG) similarly captures a hierarchy of intrinsic neural timescales (INT), as well as alterations in psychopathology (Watanabe et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the study that developed and validated the INT method.

claims.claim: The hypothesis tested was that hallucinations and delusions are associated with distinct changes of INT at low and high levels of neural hierarchies, respectively.
claims.source: Here, we specifically applied this fMRI measure to test whether hallucinations and delusions are associated with distinct changes of INT at low and high levels of neural hierarchies, respectively.
claims.evidence: This is the primary hypothesis of the study.

claims.claim: INT at low and high hierarchical levels would increase with more severe hallucinations and delusions, respectively, potentially reflecting increased neural integration of prior information.
claims.source: We hypothesized that INT at these respective levels would increase with more severe symptoms, potentially reflecting increased neural integration of prior information (Glaze et al., 2015; Mante et al., 2013; Mazurek et al., 2003), in line with behavioral findings in hallucinations and delusions (Baker et al., 2019; Cassidy et al., 2018; Powers et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citations to prior computational and behavioral studies.

claims.claim: INT changes should manifest as symptom-specific differences in hierarchical gradients.
claims.source: If present, these INT changes should manifest as symptom-specific differences in hierarchical gradients.
claims.evidence: This is a prediction derived from the hypothesis.

claims.claim: The autocorrelation function of the fMRI signal at each voxel (or vertex) was estimated and the sum of the autocorrelation coefficients during the initial positive period was calculated to estimate INT.
claims.source: Briefly, the autocorrelation function of the fMRI signal at each voxel (or vertex) was estimated and the sum of the autocorrelation coefficients during the initial positive period was calculated.
claims.evidence: This describes the methodological procedure used in the study.

claims.claim: To adjust for differences in temporal resolution, the sum of autocorrelation coefficients was multiplied by the repetition time (TR) of the fMRI data.
claims.source: To adjust for differences in temporal resolution, the sum was multiplied by the repetition time (TR) of the fMRI data.
claims.evidence: This describes a methodological adjustment made in the study.

claims.claim: INT values estimated using the sum of the initial positive period are similar to those from an exponential fit.
claims.source: note that values are similar to those from an exponential fit [Murray et al., 2014; Figure 1—figure supplement 1]
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by comparison to a prior method and by data shown in a supplementary figure.

claims.claim: INT maps were parcellated using the HCP-multimodal parcellation to facilitate further analysis.
claims.source: INT maps were parcellated using the HCP-multimodal parcellation (Glasser et al., 2016) to facilitate further analysis.
claims.evidence: This describes a methodological step in the analysis.

claims.claim: T1w/T2w (myelin) and cortical-thickness maps were obtained from high-resolution structural scans from the HCP database.
claims.source: Additionally, T1w/T2w (myelin) and cortical-thickness maps were obtained from high-resolution structural scans from the HCP database.
claims.evidence: This describes data acquisition for the study.

claims.claim: T1w/T2w and cortical thickness have previously been shown to capture an underlying brain-wide hierarchy.
claims.source: Both of these structural measures have previously been shown to capture an underlying brain-wide hierarchy (Burt et al., 2018; Fischl et al., 2008; Wagstyl et al., 2015), consistent with the classic use of myeloarchitecture and cytoarchitecture for cortical parcellation (Brodmann, 1909; Sarkissov et al., 1955; Vogt, 1911; Von Economo, 1929).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior studies.

claims.claim: Burt et al., 2018 validated T1w/T2w in macaques by showing strong agreement with a gold-standard tract-tracing measure of hierarchy.
claims.source: In particular, Burt et al., 2018 validated T1w/T2w in macaques by showing strong agreement with a gold-standard tract-tracing measure of hierarchy.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a specific validation study.

claims.claim: Burt et al. validated T1w/T2w and cortical thickness in humans against human postmortem gene-expression data, specifically using granular layer-IV-specific gene expression as a proxy for cytoarchitecture structural type.
claims.source: Establishing T1w/T2w and cortical thickness as structural indices of hierarchy in humans, Burt et al. validated these MRI measures against human postmortem gene-expression data (Hawrylycz et al., 2012)—specifically using granular layer-IV-specific gene expression as a proxy for cytoarchitecture structural type.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to validation studies.

claims.claim: In a subset of 100 unrelated young and healthy subjects from the HCP dataset, there was no systematic relationship across the whole brain between INT and the two indices of structural hierarchy (T1w/T2w and cortical thickness).
claims.source: Consistent with prior empirical and theoretical work (Chaudhuri et al., 2015; Vázquez-Rodríguez et al., 2019), in a subset of 100 unrelated young and healthy subjects from the HCP dataset, we did not observe a systematic relationship across the whole brain between INT (Figure 1A)—an index of functional hierarchy (Chaudhuri et al., 2015; Murray et al., 2014)—and the two indices of structural hierarchy (T1w/T2w and cortical thickness) (Burt et al., 2018; Fischl et al., 2008; Wagstyl et al., 2015; Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the study based on data analysis, supported by reference to figures.

claims.claim: The study focused on specific, well-studied hierarchies of the auditory, visual, and somatosensory systems that have been parcellated in humans, where the functional and structural indices of hierarchy appeared better aligned.
claims.source: We thus decided to focus on specific, well-studied hierarchies of the auditory, visual, and somatosensory systems that have been parcellated in humans, and where the functional and structural indices of hierarchy appeared better aligned.
claims.evidence: This describes a methodological decision based on the observed data patterns.

claims.claim: The winning ordering for the auditory cortex was A1 → lateral belt (LBelt) → medial belt (MBelt) → parabelt (PBelt) → retroinsular cortex (RI) → A4 → A5.
claims.source: The winning orderings were A1 → lateral belt (LBelt) → medial belt (MBelt) → parabelt (PBelt) → retroinsular cortex (RI) → A4 → A5 for the auditory cortex
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the data-driven hierarchy selection analysis.

claims.claim: The winning ordering for the visual cortex was V1 → V2 → V3 → middle temporal area (MT) → V4 → V6 → V7.
claims.source: V1 → V2 → V3 → middle temporal area (MT) → V4 → V6 → V7 for the visual cortex
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the data-driven hierarchy selection analysis.

claims.claim: The winning ordering for the somatosensory cortex was 3b → 3a → 1 → 2 → 5m → 7b → 7a.
claims.source: and 3b → 3a → 1 → 2 → 5m → 7b → 7a for the somatosensory cortex (Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the data-driven hierarchy selection analysis.

claims.claim: For all three sensory systems, area 46 was selected as the highest hierarchical level when two additional prefrontal cortex regions were added.
claims.source: For all three sensory systems, area 46 was selected as the highest hierarchical level (Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the data-driven hierarchy selection analysis.

claims.claim: Each of the PFC-extended winning models explained more variance than chance based on a null distribution of 10,000 random orderings.
claims.source: Notably, each of the PFC-extended winning models explained more variance than chance based on a null distribution of 10,000 random orderings (auditory system: Ppermutation < 10−4; visual system: Ppermutation = 0.003; somatosensory system: Ppermutation = 0.001).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical finding from permutation testing.

claims.claim: Within the HCP dataset, hierarchical position significantly correlated with INT in the auditory system (Spearman correlation rs = 0.87, p=0.005).
claims.source: Within the HCP dataset, hierarchical position significantly correlated with INT in the auditory system (Spearman correlation rs = 0.87, p=0.005; Figure 1C)
claims.evidence: This is a statistical finding from correlation analysis.

claims.claim: The correlation between hierarchical position and INT in the auditory system was above chance level based on a null distribution of 10,000 random orderings (Ppermutation = 0.003).
claims.source: and this correlation was above chance level based on a null distribution of 10,000 random orderings (Ppermutation = 0.003).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical finding from permutation testing.

claims.claim: The hierarchical ordering was validated in an out-of-sample group of 158 healthy controls from the schizophrenia combined dataset, where hierarchy similarly correlated with INT in the auditory system (rs = 0.80, p=0.01).
claims.source: The hierarchical ordering was further validated in an out-of-sample group of 158 healthy controls from the schizophrenia combined dataset (Materials and methods), where hierarchy similarly correlated with INT in the auditory system (rs = 0.80, p=0.01; Figure 1C).
claims.evidence: This is a validation finding from an independent dataset.

claims.claim: Positive but non-significant correlations were observed between hierarchical position and INT in the visual system (in-sample: rs = 0.27, p=0.49, Ppermutation = 0.47; out-of-sample: rs = 0.22, p=0.58).
claims.source: Positive but non-significant correlations were observed in the visual system (in-sample: rs = 0.27, p=0.49, Ppermutation = 0.47; out-of-sample: rs = 0.22, p=0.58; Figure 1C).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical finding from correlation analysis.

claims.claim: Stronger positive correlations were observed between hierarchical position and INT in the somatosensory system that reached significance in the out-of-sample group (in-sample: rs = 0.58, p=0.108, Ppermutation = 0.097; out-of-sample: rs = 0.80, p=0.014).
claims.source: Stronger positive correlations were observed in the somatosensory system that reached significance in the out-of-sample group (in-sample: rs = 0.58, p=0.108, Ppermutation = 0.097; out-of-sample: rs = 0.80, p=0.014; Figure 1C).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical finding from correlation analysis.

claims.claim: Expression of granular layer IV genes showed strong, negative correlations with hierarchical level in all three winning hierarchies (auditory: rs = −0.88, p=0.003; visual: rs = −0.75, p=0.026; somatosensory: rs = −0.87, p=0.005).
claims.source: Consistent with this, expression of granular layer IV genes showed strong, negative correlations with hierarchical level in all three winning hierarchies (auditory: rs = −0.88, p=0.003; visual: rs = −0.75, p=0.026; somatosensory: rs = −0.87, p=0.005; Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: This is a validation finding using independent gene expression data.

claims.claim: Extended sensory hierarchies were empirically validated that captured variability in hierarchical indices across three independent datasets.
claims.source: Thus, we empirically validated extended sensory hierarchies that captured variability in hierarchical indices across three independent datasets, although this was generally less clear for the visual system.
claims.evidence: This is a summary statement of validation findings across multiple datasets.

claims.claim: Head motion during data acquisition was associated with decreased INT values (181 out of 188 parcels, Ppermutation = 0.01).
claims.source: Head motion during data acquisition was associated with decreased INT values (181 out of 188 parcels, Ppermutation = 0.01; Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from robustness analysis examining potential confounds.

claims.claim: The effects of head motion on INT were comparable across hierarchical levels in all three sensory systems.
claims.source: Yet, these effects were comparable across hierarchical levels (auditory system: rs = −0.23, Ppermutation = 0.805; visual system: rs = −0.38, Ppermutation = 0.649; somatosensory system: rs = −0.88, Ppermutation = 0.054; Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from robustness analysis examining potential confounds.

claims.claim: No effects of gender or age on INT were observed (all Ppermutation > 0.174).
claims.source: No effects were observed for gender or age (all Ppermutation > 0.174).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from robustness analysis examining potential confounds.

claims.claim: INT maps showed excellent reliability between the first and last 5 min of the fMRI acquisition (median ICC(2,1) ± interquartile range across voxels: 0.94 ± 0.03).
claims.source: Finally, INT maps showed excellent reliability between the first and last 5 min of the fMRI acquisition (median ICC(2,1) ± interquartile range across voxels: 0.94 ± 0.03; Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from reliability analysis.

claims.claim: Compared to controls (N = 158), patients (N = 127) exhibited a small-to-moderate, but widespread, reduction of INT (98 out of 188 parcels, Ppermutation = 0.013).
claims.source: Compared to controls (N = 158), patients (N = 127) exhibited a small-to-moderate, but widespread, reduction of INT (98 out of 188 parcels, Ppermutation = 0.013; Figure 2E).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from the exploratory diagnosis analysis.

claims.claim: The INT reductions in patients were comparable across hierarchical levels (all Ppermutation > 0.40).
claims.source: However, the INT reductions in patients were comparable across hierarchical levels (all Ppermutation > 0.40; Figure 2F).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the exploratory diagnosis analysis.

claims.claim: In silico simulations using a large-scale biophysical model suggested that the global INT reduction in patients could be neuronally implemented by globally reduced excitation-inhibition (E/I) ratio.
claims.source: In silico simulations using a large-scale biophysical model (Chaudhuri et al., 2015) suggested that the global INT reduction in patients could be neuronally implemented by globally reduced excitation-inhibition (E/I) ratio (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from computational modeling simulations.

claims.claim: Patients with more severe hallucinations exhibited a less pronounced INT hierarchical gradient in the auditory system, consistent with increased timescales at lower levels.
claims.source: Patients with more severe hallucinations exhibited a less pronounced INT hierarchical gradient, consistent with increased timescales at lower levels compared to those with less severe hallucinations
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from the symptom analysis.

claims.claim: Patients with more severe delusions exhibited a more pronounced INT hierarchical gradient in the auditory and somatosensory systems, consistent with increased timescales at higher levels.
claims.source: those with more severe delusions instead exhibited a more pronounced INT hierarchical gradient, consistent with increased timescales at higher levels compared to those with less severe delusions (Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from the symptom analysis.

claims.claim: The severity of hallucinations and delusions in the sample were correlated (rs = 0.62, p<0.01) but had sufficient unique variance [(1 – R2)=0.62] to evaluate their independent contributions.
claims.source: As expected, severity of hallucinations and delusions in our sample were correlated (rs = 0.62, p<0.01) but had sufficient unique variance [(1 – R2)=0.62] to evaluate their independent contributions.
claims.evidence: This is a statistical finding describing the relationship between symptom measures.

claims.claim: The severity of hallucinations and delusions was uncorrelated with antipsychotic dose among the 109 patients with available data (chlorpromazine equivalents: both p>0.86).
claims.source: The severity of these symptoms was uncorrelated with antipsychotic dose among the 109 patients with available data (chlorpromazine equivalents: both p>0.86), making medication an unlikely confound (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from analysis of potential medication confounds.

claims.claim: The model (M2) that tested main effects and interactions of symptoms on hierarchical INT gradients was significant (omnibus F11,41 = 5.52, p<10−4).
claims.source: The model (M2; Materials and methods) that we used as a primary test of main effects and interactions of symptoms on hierarchical INT gradients—which also included interaction terms for each sensory system to account for between-system differences—was significant (omnibus F11,41 = 5.52, p<10−4).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical finding from the primary hypothesis test.

claims.claim: Hierarchical-gradient effects differed significantly between hallucinations and delusions in the auditory system (symptom-by-hierarchical-level interaction: t42 = 4.59 [95% bootstrap confidence interval: 3.39, 9.08], Cohen's f2 = 1.00, Ppermutation = 0.001).
claims.source: Critically, within this model we found hierarchical-gradient effects that differed significantly between hallucinations and delusions in the expected directions for 2/3 systems (auditory system, symptom-by-hierarchical-level interaction: t42 = 4.59 [95% bootstrap confidence interval: 3.39, 9.08], Cohen's f2 = 1.00, Ppermutation = 0.001
claims.evidence: This is a primary statistical finding supporting the main hypothesis.

claims.claim: Hierarchical-gradient effects differed between hallucinations and delusions in the somatosensory system (t42 = 3.50 [2.19, 7.35], f2 = 0.41, Ppermutation = 0.011).
claims.source: and somatosensory: t42 = 3.50 [2.19, 7.35], f2 = 0.41, Ppermutation = 0.011; Figure 3).
claims.evidence: This is a primary statistical finding supporting the main hypothesis.

claims.claim: Hierarchical-gradient effects did not differ significantly between hallucinations and delusions in the visual system (t42 = −2.06 [–6.19, 0.16], f2 = 0.11, Ppermutation = 0.083).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical finding from the primary hypothesis test.

claims.claim: In the auditory system, the symptom-by-hierarchical-level interaction was driven by significant hierarchical-gradient effects in opposite directions for hallucinations (hierarchical-level effect: t42 = −3.50 [–8.42,–2.24], f2 = 0.41, Ppermutation = 0.010) and delusions (hierarchical-level effect: t42 = 2.99 [1.18, 6.37], f2 = 0.27, Ppermutation = 0.025).
claims.source: In the auditory system, this interaction was driven by significant hierarchical-gradient effects in opposite directions for hallucinations (hierarchical-level effect: t42 = −3.50 [–8.42,–2.24], f2 = 0.41, Ppermutation = 0.010) and delusions (hierarchical-level effect: t42 = 2.99 [1.18, 6.37], f2 = 0.27, Ppermutation = 0.025).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical finding decomposing the interaction effect.

claims.claim: In the somatosensory system, the symptom-by-hierarchical-level interaction was driven by a trend-level negative hierarchical-gradient effect for hallucinations (hierarchical-level effect: t42 = −2.35 [–5.91,–1.00], f2 = 0.15, Ppermutation = 0.056) and a significant positive hierarchical-gradient effect for delusions (hierarchical-level effect: t42 = 2.60 [1.43, 5.57], f2 = 0.19, Ppermutation = 0.042).
claims.source: In the somatosensory system, this effect was driven by a trend-level negative hierarchical-gradient effect for hallucinations (hierarchical-level effect: t42 = −2.35 [–5.91,–1.00], f2 = 0.15, Ppermutation = 0.056) and a significant positive hierarchical-gradient effect for delusions (hierarchical-level effect: t42 = 2.60 [1.43, 5.57], f2 = 0.19, Ppermutation = 0.042; Figure 3).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical finding decomposing the interaction effect.

claims.claim: In the visual system, hierarchical-gradient effects were not significant for either hallucinations (t42 = 0.90 [–1.06, 3.62], f2 = 0.00, Ppermutation = 0.466) or delusions (t42 = −2.01 [–6.01, 0.53], f2 = 0.11, Ppermutation = 0.087).
claims.source: In the visual system, hierarchical-gradient effects were not significant for either symptom (hallucination hierarchical-level effect: t42 = 0.90 [–1.06, 3.62], f2 = 0.00, Ppermutation = 0.466; delusion hierarchical-level effect: t42 = −2.01 [–6.01, 0.53], f2 = 0.11, Ppermutation = 0.087).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical finding from the primary hypothesis test.

claims.claim: A family-wise permutation test showed that the observed set of results was statistically above chance (set-level Ppermutation = 0.014).
claims.source: Based on the chance level of jointly observing negative hierarchical-gradient effects of hallucination severity in at least 1/3 systems, and positive hierarchical-gradient effects of delusion severity in at least 2/3 systems, and interaction effects of hierarchy-by-symptom in the expected direction in at least 2/3 systems, this analysis suggested that the observed set of results was statistically above chance (set-level Ppermutation = 0.014).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical finding from multiple comparison correction.

claims.claim: Based on the chance level of observing all three effects (negative hierarchical-gradient for hallucinations, positive hierarchical-gradient for delusions, and significant symptom-by-hierarchical-level interaction) in one system, the observed set of results in the auditory system was statistically above chance (set-level Ppermutation = 0.043).
claims.source: Furthermore, based on the chance level of observing a significant negative hierarchical-gradient effect for hallucinations, and a significant positive hierarchical-gradient effect for delusions, and a significant symptom-by-hierarchical-level interaction (i.e. all three effects in one system), the observed set of results in the auditory system was also statistically above chance (set-level Ppermutation = 0.043).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical finding from multiple comparison correction.

claims.claim: Results were generally consistent across the different hierarchical orderings tested for each sensory system.
claims.source: Results were generally consistent across the different hierarchical orderings (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), particularly in the auditory system.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from robustness analysis testing alternative hierarchical orderings.

claims.claim: A family-wise permutation test including all four orderings per system (12 total orderings) showed that the observed set of results was statistically above chance for all systems (set-level Ppermutation = 0.002) and for the auditory system alone (set-level Ppermutation = 0.001).
claims.source: A family-wise permutation test similar to the one above, but including all four orderings per system (12 total orderings), showed that the observed set of results was statistically above chance for all systems (set-level Ppermutation = 0.002) and for the auditory system alone (set-level Ppermutation = 0.001).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical finding from robustness analysis with multiple comparison correction.

claims.claim: In the auditory system, conceptual disorganization was the only symptom—other than hallucinations and delusions—that showed a significant hierarchical-gradient effect (hierarchical-level effect: t21 = −2.80 [–5.31,–1.10], f2 = 0.60, Ppermutation = 0.036).
claims.source: In the auditory system, conceptual disorganization was the only symptom—other than hallucinations and delusions—that showed a significant effect (hierarchical-level effect: t21 = −2.80 [–5.31,–1.10], f2 = 0.60, Ppermutation = 0.036; Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from post-hoc specificity analysis.

claims.claim: The hierarchical-gradient effect of conceptual disorganization was weaker than that for hallucinations (hierarchical-level effect: t21 = −4.38 [–10.31,–3.28], f2 = 10.57, Ppermutation = 0.005).
claims.source: But this effect was weaker than that for hallucinations (hierarchical-level effect: t21 = −4.38 [–10.31,–3.28], f2 = 10.57, Ppermutation = 0.005; Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from post-hoc specificity analysis.

claims.claim: A permutation test comparing the average strength of hierarchical-gradient effects for positive versus negative symptoms showed the effects of positive symptoms to be significantly larger than the effects of negative symptoms (Ppermutation = 0.043) in the auditory system.
claims.source: Indeed, a permutation test comparing the average strength of hierarchical-gradient effects (i.e. mean absolute-value of t-statistics) for positive versus negative symptoms (i.e. blunted affect, social withdrawal, emotional withdrawal, and alogia) showed the effects of positive symptoms to be significantly larger than the effects of negative symptoms (Ppermutation = 0.043) in the auditory system.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from post-hoc specificity analysis.

claims.claim: In the somatosensory system, no symptoms other than delusions showed a significant hierarchical-gradient effect.
claims.source: In the somatosensory system, no symptoms other than delusions showed a significant hierarchical-gradient effect.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from post-hoc specificity analysis.

claims.claim: In the somatosensory system, hallucinations showed the strongest negative hierarchical-gradient effect (hierarchical-level effect: t21 = −2.23 [–6.79,–1.75], f2 = 0.31, Ppermutation = 0.079).
claims.source: Hallucinations, however, showed the strongest negative effect (hierarchical-level effect: t21 = −2.23 [–6.79,–1.75], f2 = 0.31, Ppermutation = 0.079; Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from post-hoc specificity analysis.

claims.claim: The biophysical model was able to recapitulate the INT effects of hallucinations and delusions via local increases in E/I ratio at low or high levels of the hierarchy, respectively.
claims.source: In silico results using the best-fitting parameters were able to recapitulate the INT effects of hallucinations and delusions (compression versus expansion of the INT hierarchical gradient, respectively) via local increases in E/I ratio at low or high levels of the hierarchy, respectively.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from computational modeling simulations.

claims.claim: The best-fitting levels of the peak increase in local E/I ratio were levels 1 and 8 for hallucinations and delusions, respectively.

results.result: The authors validated extended sensory hierarchies for auditory, visual, and somatosensory systems using structural MRI measures (T1w/T2w, cortical thickness) and functional INT measures across three independent datasets. The auditory and somatosensory hierarchies showed significant correlations with INT and gene expression markers, while the visual system showed weaker effects.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C44 provide convergent evidence from structural MRI, functional INT, and gene expression data across multiple independent samples (HCP N=100, schizophrenia controls N=158, and Allen Brain Atlas). The auditory hierarchy showed strong correlations (rs=0.87 in-sample, rs=0.80 out-of-sample, both p<0.05) and the somatosensory system reached significance in the out-of-sample validation (rs=0.80, p=0.014). All three systems showed significant correlations with layer IV gene expression (all p<0.05). The visual system results were weaker but this limitation is acknowledged.

results.result: INT measurements demonstrated excellent test-retest reliability (ICC=0.94±0.03) and were robust to potential confounds, with head motion effects being comparable across hierarchical levels and no significant effects of age or gender.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C48 provide statistical evidence for INT reliability and robustness. The ICC values indicate excellent reliability, and while head motion affected INT values (181/188 parcels, p=0.01), these effects were comparable across hierarchical levels (all p>0.05), which is critical for the hierarchical gradient analyses. The lack of age and gender effects (all p>0.174) further supports measurement validity.

results.result: Patients with schizophrenia showed widespread but modest reductions in INT compared to controls (98/188 parcels, p=0.013), with effects comparable across hierarchical levels. Biophysical modeling suggested this could reflect globally reduced excitation-inhibition ratio.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C51 present exploratory findings with appropriate statistical support (permutation testing p=0.013) and computational modeling interpretation. The finding that INT reductions were comparable across hierarchical levels (all p>0.40) is important for distinguishing diagnosis effects from symptom-specific effects. The biophysical modeling provides a plausible mechanistic interpretation, though this remains speculative.

results.result: Hallucinations and delusions showed distinct hierarchical INT alterations in opposite directions in the auditory and somatosensory systems. Hallucinations were associated with compressed INT gradients (increased timescales at lower levels), while delusions were associated with expanded gradients (increased timescales at higher levels). These effects survived family-wise multiple comparison correction.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C64 constitute the primary hypothesis test with robust statistical support. The omnibus model was significant (F11,41=5.52, p<10⁻⁴), and symptom-by-hierarchical-level interactions were significant in auditory (t42=4.59, p=0.001, f²=1.00) and somatosensory (t42=3.50, p=0.011, f²=0.41) systems. Individual symptom effects showed opposite directions as predicted. Family-wise permutation testing confirmed results were above chance (set-level p=0.014 for all systems, p=0.043 for auditory alone). The symptoms had sufficient unique variance (1-R²=0.62) and were uncorrelated with medication dose (both p>0.86), addressing key confounds. The visual system null result is appropriately reported.

results.result: The primary symptom findings were robust across different hierarchical orderings tested for each sensory system, with family-wise permutation testing across all 12 orderings confirming results were above chance.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C66 demonstrate robustness of the main findings to alternative hierarchy definitions. Testing across four orderings per system (12 total) with family-wise correction showed results remained significant (set-level p=0.002 for all systems, p=0.001 for auditory), particularly in the auditory system where effects were strongest. This addresses concerns about arbitrary hierarchy selection.

results.result: Post-hoc analyses showed some specificity of hierarchical-gradient effects to positive symptoms, with conceptual disorganization showing weaker effects than hallucinations in the auditory system, and positive symptoms showing significantly larger effects than negative symptoms.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C71 provide post-hoc specificity analyses with appropriate statistical testing. In the auditory system, conceptual disorganization showed significant effects (t21=-2.80, p=0.036) but weaker than hallucinations (t21=-4.38, p=0.005), and positive symptoms overall showed larger effects than negative symptoms (p=0.043). The authors appropriately note these effects don't need to be unique to hallucinations/delusions under the theoretical model, and acknowledge this as preliminary evidence requiring further investigation.

results.result: Biophysical modeling recapitulated the observed INT effects through local increases in E/I ratio at different hierarchical levels (level 1 for hallucinations requiring ΔE/I=21.61%, level 8 for delusions requiring ΔE/I=4.02%). The model suggested additivity of symptom-specific alterations could explain symptom co-occurrence, with preliminary in vivo support.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C79 present computational modeling results that qualitatively match the empirical findings. However, the modeling uses macaque visual system data to model human auditory system effects due to lack of tract-tracing data, limiting quantitative interpretation as the authors acknowledge. The additivity hypothesis is supported by modeling (C75-C76) and has preliminary in vivo support (C77-C79: higher INT in patients with both symptoms, t27=1.84, p=0.038; higher intercept, t257=2.04, p=0.043; no gradient difference, t257=0.65, p=0.519), but the in vivo analysis uses small subgroups (N=11 vs N=18) and requires replication.

results.result: Control analyses examining dorsal versus ventral auditory streams showed that delusion effects were specific to the dorsal stream (including dorsolateral PFC area 46), while hallucination effects showed trends in both streams. This supports the involvement of dorsolateral PFC in delusions.
results.evaluation: Claims C80-C88 present control analyses with appropriate validation of the ventral auditory hierarchy (correlations with INT and gene expression similar to dorsal stream) and statistical testing of stream differences. The significant symptom-by-hierarchical-level-by-processing-stream interaction (t28=1.75, p=0.005) and specific difference in delusion effects between streams (t28=1.89, p=0.003) support the interpretation, consistent with prior literature (Corlett et al., 2007).

results.result: A data-driven approach using voxels ranked by INT values replicated the main findings, showing significant symptom-by-hierarchical-level interactions (t16=5.19, p=0.003) with opposite effects for hallucinations and delusions.
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C90 provide an anatomically agnostic replication of the main findings using a data-driven hierarchy definition based on INT rankings. The significant interaction (t16=5.19, p=0.003, f²=10.12) and individual symptom effects in opposite directions (hallucinations: t16=-2.79, p=0.049; delusions: t16=4.55, p=0.008) support the robustness of findings to hierarchy definition method.
